procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of the Gujarat High Court in Criminal Revision Application No. 145 of 1964, dated November 9, 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court allowed the Criminal Revision Application No. 145 of 1964 and set aside the conviction and sentence of Manilal Maganlal (the respondent).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The License Inspector appealed to the Supreme Court by certificate granted by the High Court to challenge the High Court's decision to set aside the conviction. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and maintained the order passed by the High Court.

directions: The order passed by the High Court is maintained.

issue.issue_text: Whether a long-standing judicial interpretation from a single High Court decision should be upheld on the principle of stare decisis, even if it is erroneous.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued that a specific interpretation established by a single Bombay High Court decision in *The State v. Manilal Jethalal* had been followed for a long time without any other court taking a different view.
Based on this, the appellant contended that the Supreme Court should not disturb this long-prevailing view, invoking the principle of stare decisis (upholding precedent).
law: The principle of stare decisis is strongest when a series of decisions have established a particular view, that view has been widely accepted, and various rights have been created for parties acting in reliance on that view.
A person filing a complaint under the relevant Act must have the legal authority to do so.
application: The Supreme Court found that the conditions for applying stare decisis were not met in this case.
The Court noted that this was not a situation involving a "series of decisions" but rather a single High Court ruling.

Crucially, the Court reasoned that legal authority to file a complaint cannot be conferred by an "erroneous interpretation long acquiesced in." In other words, a long-standing mistake does not create a legal right or authority that doesn't otherwise exist.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, refusing to uphold the long-standing but erroneous interpretation from the single High Court decision. It held that an incorrect interpretation, even if accepted for a long time, cannot create legal authority where none exists under the statute.

issue.issue_text: Whether authority to file a complaint under the Act can be conferred by a long-standing but erroneous interpretation of the law.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued that a previous decision by the Bombay High Court in *The State v. Manilal Jethalal* had established a particular interpretation of the law.
The counsel contended that since this interpretation had prevailed for a long time without being challenged, the Supreme Court should not disturb it.
law: A person who files a complaint under the Act must be able to show that they have the legal authority to file that complaint.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, stating that authority to file a complaint cannot be conferred by an erroneous interpretation of the law, even if it has been accepted or "long acquiesced in."

The Court distinguished this case from situations where a long series of decisions have established a particular view and various rights have been created based on that view. Here, there was only one prior decision, not a well-established line of precedent.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court held that a long-standing but incorrect interpretation of a law cannot create legal authority where none exists. The authority to file a complaint must be based on a correct reading of the statute itself.

issue.issue_text: Whether only the authorities specifically mentioned in the Act have the power to launch proceedings for offences under the Act.

law.fact_text: The relevant sections of the Act are Section 481 and Section 69.
law.label: law

law.fact_text: The court cited a precedent, Aganwala v. J. C. Chakravarty, which held that a complaint under the Calcutta Municipal Act could only be filed by the authorities mentioned in that act, not by an ordinary citizen.
law.label: law

application.fact_text: The Court applied the logic from the Aganwala case, concluding that similarly, only the authorities mentioned in Section 481, read with Section 69, can launch proceedings under the Act in question.
application.label: application

application.fact_text: The Court rejected the appellant's argument that a long-standing, contrary interpretation from a single previous case (The State v. Manilal Jethalal) should be upheld.
application.label: application

application.fact_text: The Court reasoned that a person who files a complaint must be able to show they have the specific authority to do so under the Act.
application.label: application

application.fact_text: It further stated that such legal authority cannot be created simply because an erroneous interpretation has been accepted for a long time.
application.label: application

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that only the authorities specifically mentioned in Section 481, read with Section 69 of the Act, have the power to launch proceedings for offences under the Act. The authority to file a complaint must be explicitly granted by the statute and cannot be conferred by a long-standing but incorrect interpretation of the law.

cases.principle: A person who files a complaint under an Act must show that he has the authority to file that complaint, and that authority cannot be conferred upon him by an erroneous interpretation long acquiesced in.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A person who files a complaint under an Act must show that he has the authority to file that complaint, and that authority cannot be conferred upon him by an erroneous interpretation, even if it has been long acquiesced in.
obiter: The principle of not disturbing a long-held legal view does not apply where it is not a case of a series of decisions having been taken, and where various rights have not accrued to parties acting on that view.
The court is not free to interpret words in a statute to mean something different from their ordinary meaning in the English language.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Only the authorities specifically mentioned in the Act have the power to launch proceedings for offences under the Act. A person who files a complaint must demonstrate they have this statutory authority, and such authority cannot be conferred by a long-standing but erroneous judicial interpretation.
legal_tests_applied: For the principle of stare decisis to apply to a long-standing view, it must be a case where 'a series of decisions have taken a particular view and that view has been widely accepted and various right• have accrued :o par-ties acting on that view.'
A person who files a complaint under the Act must show that he has the authority to file that complaint.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's stare decisis argument because the precedent was a single High Court decision, not a series of widely accepted decisions upon which various rights had been built.
The court held that authority to file a complaint cannot be conferred by an erroneous interpretation of the law, even if it has been long acquiesced in.
why_respondent_won: The court determined that only the authorities specifically mentioned in the Act could launch proceedings, and the complaint in this case was not filed by such an authority.
The court affirmed the principle that a complainant must have actual statutory authority, which cannot be created by a mistaken judicial precedent.
policy_considerations: The principle of stare decisis is not absolute and should not be used to perpetuate an error from a single decision, especially when it does not involve a situation where a series of decisions have been widely accepted and have led to the accrual of rights by various parties.
